b: Cost per sale (CPS) is the amount an advertiser spends for each sale its advertising generates. The term has two uses that share one idea. As a metric, it is marketing cost divided by the number of sales in a period. As a pricing model, it describes a deal in which the advertiser pays a media owner, publisher or creator only when a referred customer completes a purchase. Both exist for the same reason: online sellers earn money per transaction, and they want to know, or contractually fix, what each transaction cost to win.

The arithmetic is a single division. AppsFlyer's glossary gives the formula as total marketing and sales cost divided by number of sales, with the example of USD 5,000 in costs and 200 sales producing a cost per sale of USD 25. The simplicity hides three decisions that change the result.
The first is the numerator. AppsFlyer's version includes sales salaries and marketing materials; most ad platform reporting counts media spend alone.

The second is the denominator. A "sale" can be a gross order on the day of purchase or a net order after cancellations and returns. Affiliate programmes usually count only validated sales, so the cost per sale an advertiser calculates from its shop analytics on day one will rarely match what a network invoices weeks later.

The third is attribution. Each platform credits sales to itself under its own lookback window and counting rules. Summed across platforms, credited sales often exceed the sales a shop actually recorded, which pushes every platform's cost per sale down.

A worked example shows how the metric links to others. A shop spends EUR 6,000 on search ads in a month and credits 400 sales to them, a cost per sale of EUR 15. With an average order value (AOV) of EUR 60, revenue is EUR 24,000, return on ad spend (ROAS) is 4.0 and the cost-to-revenue ratio is 25%. If the gross margin on that basket is 30%, each sale earns EUR 18 before advertising, so the EUR 15 cost per sale leaves EUR 3 of contribution. Any cost per sale above EUR 18 loses money on the first purchase.

In the pricing sense, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) defines pay-per-sale as a model in which advertisers pay agencies or media companies "based on how many sales transactions were generated as a direct result of the ad", according to the Coalition for Innovative Media Measurement dictionary, which cites the IAB. The affiliate platform impact.com describes CPS as "essentially a subset of CPA", used where the audience must complete a sale rather than a lead or sign-up.
The mechanics follow a fixed sequence:
A publisher, creator or network receives a tracking link or code tied to its account.
A shopper clicks the link, and the click is recorded with a timestamp, usually in a cookie, URL parameter or platform login.
If the shopper buys within the attribution window, the merchant's checkout fires a conversion event carrying the order value.
The sale enters a pending state while the merchant waits out the return or cancellation period.
Once validated, the commission is calculated, either as a fixed fee per sale or as a percentage of order value, and paid on a set cycle.

Commission rates vary by category. Amazon's Associates programme pays standard referral rates of 10% on luxury beauty, 4.5% on physical books, kitchen and automotive, and 3% on toys, home, beauty and sports, with a 24-hour window from the click, as PPC Land's Amazon Influencer Program explainer lists. Payment lags are long. When Amazon products became taggable through the YouTube Shopping affiliate programme, commissions locked monthly and paid two AdSense cycles later, with returns deducted from the current balance.

The commercial logic is a transfer of risk. Under cost-per-click or cost-per-thousand pricing, the advertiser pays whether or not anyone buys. Under cost per sale, the publisher carries conversion risk, and prices it in through higher effective rates or by promoting only products that convert.

Paying per sale predates the acronym. Amazon's own FAQ once claimed its Associates programme, launched in July 1996, was the first affiliate programme on the internet. Shawn Collins disputed that in a November 2000 history for ClickZ, citing PC Flowers & Gifts in October 1994 and an informal CDNow programme the same year. Networks such as LinkShare, Be Free and Commission Junction followed between 1996 and 1998.

Search platforms experimented with the model next. On March 20, 2007, Google announced a pay-per-action beta in which US advertisers on its content network paid a fixed price only for a completed action, citing "$5 when a purchase is made" as an example, according to the Inside AdWords blog. Google retired the beta in the last week of August 2008, pointing advertisers to Conversion Optimizer and to the Google Affiliate Network, the former DoubleClick Performics network it had acquired with DoubleClick, according to a June 30, 2008 post.

Per-sale pricing returned in narrower forms. Google Shopping Actions, launched on March 19, 2018, took a share of a retailer's sale only when a shopper bought, according to TechCrunch. Google dropped that commission in July 2020, according to Social Media Today, and closed what had become Buy on Google on September 26, 2023, according to Google's Ads Developer Blog. Etsy's Offsite Ads, billed since April 14, 2020, charge 15% of an attributed order for shops under USD 10,000 in annual sales and 12% above it, capped at USD 100.

The fastest recent growth has come from creator commerce. YouTube said in September 2026 that commission payouts to creators had doubled year on year, with more than 1.3 million channels enrolled in YouTube Shopping. No base figure or currency was given.

Cost per sale is the figure that connects a media plan to a profit and loss account. Ecommerce teams use it to compare channels and set seasonal bids. It also moves with the market. Channable, which manages product feeds for more than 10,000 European shops, found the median Google Ads cost per sale rose 14%, from EUR 14.41 in October 2025 to EUR 16.47 in October 2026, while click prices were broadly flat. Click-through rates rose and conversion rates fell in most categories, so the increase came from fewer clicks turning into purchases rather than from dearer clicks. In Germany, Performance Max cost per sale rose 25%.
As a pricing model, CPS shapes how budgets flow to creators and publishers. Taboola framed its creator network around the principle that brands pay only for sales, not social impressions.

The metric counts every sale once, whatever its size. A EUR 20 sale and a EUR 200 sale carry equal weight, so a falling cost per sale can coincide with falling revenue if the basket mix shifts. It also ignores whether the buyer is new. Returning customers frequently buy without an ad, so a blended figure can flatter campaigns that harvest existing demand.
Incrementality is the deeper problem. A platform-reported cost per sale divides spend by sales the platform credits to itself, not by sales the advertising caused.

As a contract, CPS invites attribution disputes. Whoever records the last click before checkout collects the commission, which rewards coupon sites and browser extensions positioned at the final step. The litigation over Honey, the PayPal-owned extension accused of overwriting creators' affiliate tags at checkout, rests on that structure, as PPC Land's affiliate explainer sets out.
Cost per sale and adjacent terms

Cost per acquisition (CPA): the cost of any defined conversion, which may be a lead, sign-up, install or purchase. Cost per sale is the purchase-only case; PPC Land's Target CPA explainer covers Google's bid strategy of that name.

Cost per order (CPO): in practice often the same calculation, with CPO more common in German-language marketing and in retail reporting. PPC Land's cost per order explainer notes that affiliate contracts use both labels and the line between them is loose.

ACOS (advertising cost of sales): Amazon's ratio of ad spend to attributed sales revenue, expressed as a percentage. Despite the similar name it measures cost per unit of revenue, not per transaction, as PPC Land's ACOS entry explains.

Cost of sale (COS): a percentage of revenue used by some retargeting and affiliate platforms, equivalent to the cost-revenue ratio. In accounting, cost of sales means the direct cost of goods sold, unrelated to advertising.

On November 24, 2026, Taboola said its Howl creator network, acquired in August through its Connexity shopping unit, connected more than 60 brands with more than 21,000 creators on a sales-only payment basis, and had produced more than USD 1.5 billion in gross sales, with no period stated. No commission rates were disclosed.

A day later, Channable's benchmark put the median European Google Ads cost per sale at EUR 16.47 for October 2026. "If October was the rehearsal, this will be the most expensive Black Friday per sale we've measured in our benchmark," Rob van Nuenen, Channable's chief executive, said in the PPC Land report. He forecast more than 20% higher costs per order over the Black Friday weekend, a projection rather than a measurement.
Early Black Friday data pointed to lower volume: ProfitMetrics reported today a 10.8% fall in orders against Black Friday 2025 across the shops it tracks, but published no cost figures.

Who: Ecommerce advertisers and their agencies measure cost per sale; affiliate networks, marketplaces such as Amazon and Etsy, creator platforms such as YouTube and Taboola's Howl, and briefly Google, have sold media on a per-sale basis; feed and analytics firms such as Channable publish benchmarks.

What: The cost of each sale produced by advertising, used as an efficiency metric (marketing cost divided by sales) and as a pricing model in which the advertiser pays only for completed purchases, by fixed fee or percentage.

When: Per-sale affiliate payments date to 1994 to 1996; Google tested pay-per-action from 2007 to 2008 and per-sale shopping commissions from 2018 to 2020; Channable's latest benchmark covers October 2026.
Where: Search, shopping, affiliate, retail media and creator commerce channels, with wide use in European ecommerce reporting.

Why: Online sellers earn money per transaction, and cost per sale set against order value and margin shows whether advertising pays for itself, though it ignores basket size, customer type and incrementality, and its contract form invites disputes over who caused each sale.
